Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Frontend Development for DApps

Frontend Development for DApps

Make blockchain interactions clear, safe, and responsive for users by wiring provider, signer, contract calls, and state updates.

In this lesson
Detect provider, connect wallet, perform reads and writes, handle network and account events, and keep UI state synchronized.
Provider
An interface to the blockchain and user's wallet. Example: MetaMask.
Signer
Represents a connected account that can sign transactions and change state.
Read vs Write
View functions read state for free; state-changing functions require gas and a signature.
Key Takeaway

The frontend must separate provider roles: use a provider for reads and a signer for writes, and always show clear feedback when transactions are pending.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Provider, Signer, Contract — how they connect.
Think of the provider as a window to the network, the signer as the key holder, and the contract as a remote API you call. Your frontend coordinates these three roles.

Connect Wallet
Detect MetaMask and request account access using eth_requestAccounts.
Read & Write
Use provider for view functions; use signer for transactions that change state.

Show pending states, handle network change, and choose polling or events for synchronization.

screens.title: Web3 Provider: detect and connect
screens.narratorSegment: A Web3 provider gives your frontend an entry point to the blockchain and the user's wallet. In practice this is often a browser extension such as MetaMask that injects a provider object your code can detect. The detection step is straightforward: check for the provider object and show a clear message if none is available. Then request account access with a standard call so the wallet can present a permission prompt. An example: calling the request method to ask for accounts returns an array of addresses if the user grants permission. This provider is sufficient to read view functions because reads do not require a signer or gas. However, to send transactions you must obtain a signer from the provider after the user connects. A common misconception is treating the provider as a signer; the provider can read and relay queries, but a signer is required to sign and submit state-changing transactions. As a concrete example, detecting window. ethereum and then calling eth_requestAccounts lets you show the connected account on screen. Always handle cases where the user declines or where the provider is absent by showing installation instructions and not assuming access. Key takeaway: detect the provider, ask for permission, and then use separate provider and signer roles to keep reads and writes explicit.

keyIdea.text: Check for a provider and only then request accounts; use the provider for reads and obtain a signer for writes.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Web3 Provider
Definition

Detect and connect a provider

A provider is the bridge between your frontend and the blockchain; detect it, request account access, and handle denial or absence gracefully.

Concrete example
Check for a provider object and call eth_requestAccounts to let the wallet show a permission prompt; if approved, store the returned account address for the UI.
Common misconception
Do not assume the provider is a signer. The provider enables reads; you must obtain a signer from it to sign transactions and submit state changes.
Quick checklist
  • Check for provider existence.
  • Request account access and handle denial.
  • Store account and obtain signer when needed.
Key Takeaway

Detect the provider and ask for permission before assuming access. Use provider for reads and signer for writes to avoid security and UX mistakes.

Illustration
Sample detection pseudo-code (read-only display):
// Pseudo-code
if (window.ethereum) {
  // provider available
  const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
  // request accounts when user triggers connect
  // provider.request or eth_requestAccounts triggers permission prompt
} else {
  // show message: install MetaMask
}
Use this pattern to avoid assuming a provider exists and to provide installation guidance when needed.

screens.title: Ethers.js vs Web3.js
screens.narratorSegment: Two widely used libraries let your frontend talk to the Ethereum Virtual Machine: Web3. js and Ethers. js. Both provide provider abstractions, contract instantiation with an ABI and address, and utilities for encoding and decoding contract calls. Ethers. js is often preferred for a few practical reasons: a cleaner A P I surface, smaller and more modular packages, stronger TypeScript support, and a design that encourages explicit signer usage. Web3. js is mature and feature-rich, but it can be heavier and less focused on modern TypeScript patterns. A concrete example: creating a contract instance in Ethers. js typically involves passing the ABI, address, and either a provider or signer depending on whether you're reading or writing. A common misconception is that the library automatically manages signatures — it does not. You must explicitly use a signer for state changes. For a small demo or teaching project, either library will work, but for production code where type safety and explicit signer management matter, Ethers. js is the pragmatic choice. Closing question: which library aligns best with your project's needs for type safety and modular dependency management?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Ethers.js vs Web3.js
Ethers.js

Cleaner API, TypeScript-friendly

Ethers.js encourages explicit separation between provider and signer, has modular packages and good TypeScript types, and is commonly chosen for modern DApps.

Example usage
const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider);
// for writes:
const signer = await provider.getSigner();
const writeContract = contract.connect(signer);
Web3.js

Mature and feature-rich

Web3.js provides a wide feature set and has long been the standard; it works well but may be heavier and less focused on modern type systems.

Considerations
  • API surface can feel larger and less modular.
  • TypeScript support historically weaker than Ethers.js.
  • Both libraries require explicit signer usage for transactions.
Key takeaway

Choose the library that fits your team and tooling. For cleaner, type-safe code in modern workflows, Ethers.js is often a better fit; both require explicit signer handling.

screens.title: Connect flow in React (practical example)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a typical React connect flow and what each piece achieves. The application first checks for a provider object. If present, it creates a provider wrapper and listens for account and chain change events so the UI reacts when the user switches accounts or networks. When a user chooses to connect, the frontend calls the method that asks the wallet to share accounts, then stores the first account and fetches a signer from the provider. The signer represents the user's key and is required to sign transactions. Practically, after connecting you often call provider. getNetwork to display the network name. A common pitfall is failing to unsubscribe from events when a component unmounts; this can leave stale listeners. Another mistake is not handling the case where the user declines the permission prompt — catch the error and show a clear message. A concrete example is the DAppConnector snippet: it creates BrowserProvider, sets provider state, registers on accountsChanged and chainChanged listeners, and implements connectWallet which requests accounts, sets signer, and reads network name. Closing question: after connecting, how will you ensure the UI re-fetches contract data so the displayed values match the chain state?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Connect Flow
Snippet explained

Core steps

  • Create a provider from the injected wallet object and store it in state.
  • Listen for accountsChanged to update the displayed account and signer.
  • Listen for chainChanged and reload or reinitialize network-dependent data.
  • Request accounts on user action and call provider.getSigner to acquire a signer.
Misconception
Reloading the page on chain change is a recommended pattern for simplicity, but you can also programmatically reinitialize components if you manage all dependent state carefully.
Tip

Always clean up event listeners in a useEffect cleanup to avoid duplicated handlers and memory leaks.

Code panel (readable)
// Simplified pattern
useEffect(() => {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
    setProvider(provider);
    window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
    window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', () => window.location.reload());
  } else {
    setError('MetaMask not detected');
  }
  return () => {
    if (window.ethereum) {
      window.ethereum.removeListener('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
      window.ethereum.removeListener('chainChanged', () => {});
    }
  };
}, []);
This compact snippet shows provider creation and event registration. Remember to set signer after the user connects when you need to send transactions.

screens.title: Reading contract data (view/pure functions)
screens.narratorSegment: Reading data from a smart contract uses view or pure functions that do not change blockchain state and therefore do not require gas or a signature. To read, your frontend creates a contract instance with an ABI and address and passes a provider as the backend interface. The contract instance exposes the view methods you can call directly and await a result. A concrete example is calling a getCount function on a Counter contract to display its current value. This call is quick and free because it is executed locally via the provider and the node, without creating a transaction. A common misconception is assuming reads are always instantaneous; reads can be delayed if the node is slow or the network is congested, so the UI should show loading states. Also, if you later submit transactions that change state, remember to re-fetch the view results after confirmation so the UI reflects the new on-chain value. Example code in Ethers. js: new Contract(address, abi, provider) then call contract. getCount and convert the returned BigNumber to a string for display. Key takeaway: use provider-backed contract instances for read-only functions and always handle loading and potential node delays.

keyIdea.text: Use a provider-backed contract instance to call view or pure functions, show loading states, and re-fetch after transactions update state.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Reading Contract Data
Definition

Call view/pure functions

Instantiate a contract with ABI and address, pass a provider, and call read-only methods to display on-chain data without gas.

Concrete example
Call getCount on a Counter contract using a provider-backed contract instance and convert the returned number to a string for display.
UI note
Always show a loading indicator while waiting for the provider to return data. Handle errors when the node is unreachable.
Key Takeaway

Reads do not cost gas and use a provider. Re-fetch after state changes so UI stays in sync with the chain.

Code example
// Reading with Ethers.js
const contract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, provider);
try {
  const value = await contract.getCount();
  // convert to string for display
  displayCount(value.toString());
} catch (err) {
  setError('Error reading contract data');
}
This pattern works for any view or pure function. Keep the ABI correct and handle node or provider errors.

screens.title: Sending transactions (signer and gas)
screens.narratorSegment: Sending a transaction from the frontend involves several steps that must be clear to both code and user. First ensure a signer is available by asking the provider for one after the user connects. Then instantiate the contract with the signer so methods that change state are signed and transmitted on the user's behalf. When you call a state-changing function, the wallet will present a signature request; if the user confirms, the transaction is broadcast and you receive a transaction hash. Important: transactions need gas and can take time to be mined. Your code should await confirmation by calling the transaction's wait method or subscribing to a receipt, then re-fetch contract state after confirmation. Always catch errors: if the user rejects the signature, the library will throw an error with a recognizable code; handle it by showing a friendly message like transaction cancelled. A common error is assuming a transaction succeeds on submission; you must wait for confirmation before updating UI state. Concrete example: call contract. increment() with the signer attached, log the hash, await tx. wait, then refresh the displayed count. Key takeaway: require explicit signer usage, inform the user during pending periods, and only update state after confirmation to avoid inconsistent UI.

keyIdea.text: Use a signer to send transactions, show pending feedback, and re-fetch or wait for transaction confirmation before updating UI state.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Sending Transactions
Process

Submit a state-changing call

  1. Ensure user has connected and you have a signer.
  2. Instantiate contract with signer for write operations.
  3. Call the state-changing method; the wallet prompts the user to sign.
  4. Receive transaction hash and await confirmation with tx.wait.
  5. Re-fetch on-chain data and update UI after confirmation.
Concrete example
Call increment on your Counter contract using contractWithSigner.increment(), alert or display the hash, and wait for confirmation before showing the updated count.
UX patterns

Communicate cost and latency

  • Show a pending indicator and transaction hash while waiting.
  • Explain gas costs before asking the user to sign.
  • Provide success or failure messages and allow retry on failure.
Common mistake

Do not update the UI immediately after sending; wait for confirmation or you risk showing inaccurate on-chain state.

screens.title: Handle account and network changes
screens.narratorSegment: Users can switch accounts or networks at any time. Your DApp must detect these changes and respond predictably. Two common events from browser wallets are accountsChanged and chainChanged. When accountsChanged fires, you should update the displayed account and signer or clear them if the user disconnected. When chainChanged fires, the recommended simple approach is to reload the application so all network-dependent data is reinitialized. A more advanced approach is to reinitialize providers, fetch the new network name, and re-create contract instances. A common misconception is ignoring these events and assuming the account or network will remain constant; that leads to confusing behavior when a user tries to sign a transaction from an account that is no longer active or on the wrong network. A concrete example: if your DApp targets Polygon and the user connects on a different chain, show a clear message and offer guidance to switch networks using wallet_switchEthereumChain when appropriate. Always handle event removal on component unmount to avoid duplicate handlers. Closing reflection: how will you surface network mismatches so users do not accidentally pay gas on the wrong chain?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Account & Network Changes
Accounts

Update signer and account

When accountsChanged emits, set the new account and get a signer for that address. If accounts array is empty, treat it as a disconnect.

Example handling
If accountsChanged returns no accounts, clear account and signer state so UI shows a disconnected state and prompts the user to reconnect.
Chain

Respond to chainChanged

Reload the app or reinitialize network-dependent providers and contract instances. Notify users when they're on an unsupported network and guide them to switch.

UX Tip

Make network requirements visible early and show a clear error if the user is on the wrong chain to avoid accidental gas costs.

Cleanup
Remove event listeners on component unmount to avoid duplicated handlers and memory leaks. This keeps your app stable when users navigate between pages.

screens.title: State management: Polling vs Event Listening
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common ways to keep a DApp UI synchronized: polling and event listening. Polling repeatedly calls a view function at intervals to refresh state. It's simple to implement and works well for demos, but it makes repeated requests even when nothing changes. Event listening subscribes to contract events such as Transfer or custom events the contract emits; when a relevant event fires, the frontend reacts and re-fetches state. Event listening is more efficient because it reacts to changes only when they occur, but it requires a stable event source and careful handling of missed events when the user is offline. A hybrid approach is common: use polling on short intervals for UI freshness and event listeners to react to specific important changes. Concrete example: listen for a Transfer event to update a token balance or poll getBalance every few seconds in simple demos. Misconception: relying solely on events can miss past events emitted while the user was offline; combine with occasional polling or backend indexing for production systems. Closing takeaway: choose polling for simplicity, events for efficiency, and combine them if you need both reliability and responsiveness.

narration.text: There are two common ways to keep a DApp UI synchronized: polling and event listening. Polling repeatedly calls a view function at intervals to refresh state. It's simple to implement and works well for demos, but it makes repeated requests even when nothing changes. Event listening subscribes to contract events such as Transfer or custom events the contract emits; when a relevant event fires, the frontend reacts and re-fetches state. Event listening is more efficient because it reacts to changes only when they occur, but it requires a stable event source and careful handling of missed events when the user is offline. A hybrid approach is common: use polling on short intervals for UI freshness and event listeners to react to specific important changes. Concrete example: listen for a Transfer event to update a token balance or poll getBalance every few seconds in simple demos. Misconception: relying solely on events can miss past events emitted while the user was offline; combine with occasional polling or backend indexing for production systems. Closing takeaway: choose polling for simplicity, events for efficiency, and combine them if you need both reliability and responsiveness.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Polling vs Events
Polling

Simple periodic refresh

Call view functions on a timer to refresh displayed values. Works well for demos and small apps but can create extra load.

Example: setInterval to call getCount every 5 to 10 seconds and update the UI.
Event Listening

React to contract events

Subscribe to contract events like Transfer and update UI only when events relevant to the user occur. Efficient but needs careful handling when the frontend was offline.

Example: contract.on('Transfer', (from, to, amount) => { if (to === user) fetchBalance(); })
Combined approach

Use events for immediate reactions and occasional polling to catch missed events while the user was offline. For production, consider a backend indexer if you must guarantee no missed updates.

screens.title: Common mistakes and error handling
screens.narratorSegment: Frontends that interact with wallets must be defensive and show clear feedback. A recurring issue is not catching user-rejected transactions: when a user closes a wallet popup or rejects a signature, the underlying library typically throws an error with a specific code. Your code should catch that error and display a friendly message such as transaction cancelled or signature rejected rather than a generic failure. Another common mistake is exposing private keys or performing signing in the frontend; never do this. Also, forgetting to handle chain or account changes leads to broken flows when a user switches networks mid-session. For network switching, you can guide users to change networks with the wallet_switchEthereumChain call, but always handle the case where the request is denied. For read errors, show retry options and explain that the node may be unreachable. A concrete UX rule: clearly separate pending, success, and error states and log errors for debugging while showing calm, actionable messages to users. Closing question: what message will your app show when a user cancels a signature so the UX indicates cancellation and not a blockchain failure?

User rejections

Treat rejection as user choice

When a user rejects a transaction, catch the error and show a clear message like 'Transaction cancelled by user' instead of a generic failure notice.

Security

Never expose private keys

All signing must occur inside the user's wallet. Never copy or store private keys in the frontend.

If your DApp requires a specific network, show instructions or prompt the wallet to switch chains. Handle refusal gracefully and allow users to continue in a read-only mode where possible.

screens.title: Putting it together: front-end architecture for a DApp
screens.narratorSegment: A robust DApp frontend is organized into clear layers: the provider and signer layer, the contract abstraction layer, the UI layer, and an optional backend for indexing or off-chain data. The provider and signer layer handles wallet integration and exposes interfaces for reads and writes. The contract layer holds ABI and address, creates instances with provider or signer, and exposes neat helper functions your UI calls. The UI layer uses React state and hooks to manage display, loading states, and transaction flows. For more complex apps add a backend indexer to track historical events reliably and serve compact APIs to the frontend. A common misconception is that the frontend alone can reliably index past events; while possible for simple demos, production apps often require an indexing service to prevent missed events and improve performance. Concrete scenario: a token dashboard that shows balances, recent transfers, and pending transactions will use provider-backed read calls for balances, event listeners for new transfers, and a backend service to fetch historical activity efficiently. Closing thought: design your frontend so each layer has a single responsibility — wallet access, contract interaction, UI rendering, and optional indexing — this makes testing and maintenance far easier.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on how your web frontend becomes the user's window into the blockchain. You will learn to detect and connect a Web3 provider such as MetaMask, choose and use a JavaScript library like Ethers. js, and implement both read-only calls and state-changing transactions. We'll cover the practical mechanics — provider versus signer — and the UX patterns that keep users informed while waiting for blockchain confirmation. Throughout, you'll see concrete examples for React, including how to display an account, fetch a contract value, and send a transaction that asks the wallet to sign. We'll also address common pitfalls: handling network changes, reacting to account disconnects, and deciding between polling and event listening to keep a UI in sync. By the end, you will be able to wire a basic DApp that reads a contract, asks the user to sign changes, and updates the UI reliably after confirmation. Think about a simple counter contract: this chapter shows the exact frontend steps to show the count and let a user increment it securely and clearly.

These objectives map to practical frontend skills you will use building DApps. First, you will be able to detect and connect a user's Web3 provider so your app can request account access. For example, you'll learn how to detect a browser wallet and call the method that asks the user to expose an account. Second, you'll learn to use a JavaScript library — we focus on Ethers. js — to create provider and signer objects, instantiate contract interfaces using an ABI and address, and call functions. Third, you'll implement reading state from contracts using view or pure functions without gas and sending signed transactions for state changes using a signer. Finally, you'll manage DApp state and UX: showing pending transactions, handling network switching and account changes, and updating the UI after confirmations. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual reminder so you remember the workflow: detect, connect, call, and confirm.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on tasks you'll carry out to reach the chapter goals. You will implement a connect flow that requests accounts and listens for account and network changes. You will instantiate a contract using an ABI and address and write functions to read view data and send transactions using a signer. You will add clear UX: pending indicators, success or failure messages, and guidance for network switching. Finally, you'll choose a state strategy — simple polling for a small demo or event listeners for production—and practice re-fetching data after transaction confirmation. Each objective pairs a short why-this-matters statement so you can prioritize reliability and security when wiring frontend logic. These implementation skills map directly to the hands-on activity where you connect MetaMask, show a counter value, and implement an increment button that asks the user to sign a transaction.

A Web3 provider gives your frontend an entry point to the blockchain and the user's wallet. In practice this is often a browser extension such as MetaMask that injects a provider object your code can detect. The detection step is straightforward: check for the provider object and show a clear message if none is available. Then request account access with a standard call so the wallet can present a permission prompt. An example: calling the request method to ask for accounts returns an array of addresses if the user grants permission. This provider is sufficient to read view functions because reads do not require a signer or gas. However, to send transactions you must obtain a signer from the provider after the user connects. A common misconception is treating the provider as a signer; the provider can read and relay queries, but a signer is required to sign and submit state-changing transactions. As a concrete example, detecting window. ethereum and then calling eth_requestAccounts lets you show the connected account on screen. Always handle cases where the user declines or where the provider is absent by showing installation instructions and not assuming access. Key takeaway: detect the provider, ask for permission, and then use separate provider and signer roles to keep reads and writes explicit.

Two widely used libraries let your frontend talk to the Ethereum Virtual Machine: Web3. js and Ethers. js. Both provide provider abstractions, contract instantiation with an ABI and address, and utilities for encoding and decoding contract calls. Ethers. js is often preferred for a few practical reasons: a cleaner A P I surface, smaller and more modular packages, stronger TypeScript support, and a design that encourages explicit signer usage. Web3. js is mature and feature-rich, but it can be heavier and less focused on modern TypeScript patterns. A concrete example: creating a contract instance in Ethers. js typically involves passing the ABI, address, and either a provider or signer depending on whether you're reading or writing. A common misconception is that the library automatically manages signatures — it does not. You must explicitly use a signer for state changes. For a small demo or teaching project, either library will work, but for production code where type safety and explicit signer management matter, Ethers. js is the pragmatic choice. Closing question: which library aligns best with your project's needs for type safety and modular dependency management?

Let's walk through a typical React connect flow and what each piece achieves. The application first checks for a provider object. If present, it creates a provider wrapper and listens for account and chain change events so the UI reacts when the user switches accounts or networks. When a user chooses to connect, the frontend calls the method that asks the wallet to share accounts, then stores the first account and fetches a signer from the provider. The signer represents the user's key and is required to sign transactions. Practically, after connecting you often call provider. getNetwork to display the network name. A common pitfall is failing to unsubscribe from events when a component unmounts; this can leave stale listeners. Another mistake is not handling the case where the user declines the permission prompt — catch the error and show a clear message. A concrete example is the DAppConnector snippet: it creates BrowserProvider, sets provider state, registers on accountsChanged and chainChanged listeners, and implements connectWallet which requests accounts, sets signer, and reads network name. Closing question: after connecting, how will you ensure the UI re-fetches contract data so the displayed values match the chain state?

Reading data from a smart contract uses view or pure functions that do not change blockchain state and therefore do not require gas or a signature. To read, your frontend creates a contract instance with an ABI and address and passes a provider as the backend interface. The contract instance exposes the view methods you can call directly and await a result. A concrete example is calling a getCount function on a Counter contract to display its current value. This call is quick and free because it is executed locally via the provider and the node, without creating a transaction. A common misconception is assuming reads are always instantaneous; reads can be delayed if the node is slow or the network is congested, so the UI should show loading states. Also, if you later submit transactions that change state, remember to re-fetch the view results after confirmation so the UI reflects the new on-chain value. Example code in Ethers. js: new Contract(address, abi, provider) then call contract. getCount and convert the returned BigNumber to a string for display. Key takeaway: use provider-backed contract instances for read-only functions and always handle loading and potential node delays.

Sending a transaction from the frontend involves several steps that must be clear to both code and user. First ensure a signer is available by asking the provider for one after the user connects. Then instantiate the contract with the signer so methods that change state are signed and transmitted on the user's behalf. When you call a state-changing function, the wallet will present a signature request; if the user confirms, the transaction is broadcast and you receive a transaction hash. Important: transactions need gas and can take time to be mined. Your code should await confirmation by calling the transaction's wait method or subscribing to a receipt, then re-fetch contract state after confirmation. Always catch errors: if the user rejects the signature, the library will throw an error with a recognizable code; handle it by showing a friendly message like transaction cancelled. A common error is assuming a transaction succeeds on submission; you must wait for confirmation before updating UI state. Concrete example: call contract. increment() with the signer attached, log the hash, await tx. wait, then refresh the displayed count. Key takeaway: require explicit signer usage, inform the user during pending periods, and only update state after confirmation to avoid inconsistent UI.

Users can switch accounts or networks at any time. Your DApp must detect these changes and respond predictably. Two common events from browser wallets are accountsChanged and chainChanged. When accountsChanged fires, you should update the displayed account and signer or clear them if the user disconnected. When chainChanged fires, the recommended simple approach is to reload the application so all network-dependent data is reinitialized. A more advanced approach is to reinitialize providers, fetch the new network name, and re-create contract instances. A common misconception is ignoring these events and assuming the account or network will remain constant; that leads to confusing behavior when a user tries to sign a transaction from an account that is no longer active or on the wrong network. A concrete example: if your DApp targets Polygon and the user connects on a different chain, show a clear message and offer guidance to switch networks using wallet_switchEthereumChain when appropriate. Always handle event removal on component unmount to avoid duplicate handlers. Closing reflection: how will you surface network mismatches so users do not accidentally pay gas on the wrong chain?

There are two common ways to keep a DApp UI synchronized: polling and event listening. Polling repeatedly calls a view function at intervals to refresh state. It's simple to implement and works well for demos, but it makes repeated requests even when nothing changes. Event listening subscribes to contract events such as Transfer or custom events the contract emits; when a relevant event fires, the frontend reacts and re-fetches state. Event listening is more efficient because it reacts to changes only when they occur, but it requires a stable event source and careful handling of missed events when the user is offline. Misconception: relying solely on events can miss past events emitted while the user was offline; combine with occasional polling or backend indexing for production systems. Closing takeaway: choose polling for simplicity, events for efficiency, and combine them if you need both reliability and responsiveness.
